::: {.epigraph}
*"Here as he walked by on the 16th of October 1843, Sir William Rowan Hamilton, in a flash of genius, discovered the fundamental formula for quaternion multiplication $i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1$ & cut it on a stone of this bridge."*

[— plaque on Broom Bridge, Dublin]{.attribution}
:::

Quaternions have a public relations problem that is almost two centuries old. They are four-dimensional numbers, which already sounds like a provocation; their multiplication refuses to commute, which feels like a betrayal; and the standard introduction — here is a table, $ij = k$, $ji = -k$, memorize it — manages to make one of the most geometric objects in mathematics feel like an arbitrary list of rules. If you have met quaternions before and bounced off, the problem was almost certainly not you. It was that nobody showed you what the multiplication *looks like*.

That is the whole goal of this post. Not the rules first — the picture first. By the end, I want you to be able to read a product like $i \cdot j = k$ and *see* a specific, rigid motion of a four-dimensional sphere, using nothing but your ordinary three-dimensional imagination. The trick for pulling this off is one of my favorite maneuvers in all of mathematics: when you cannot see a space, drop down a dimension, and practice empathy for the creature who cannot see *yours*.

A debt, before we start. The visualization this post builds — the dimensional ladder, the projected hypersphere, the right-hand rule for the double rotation — I learned from Grant Sanderson's video on quaternions [@sanderson2018quaternions], which I genuinely consider one of the best pieces of math exposition ever made; he and Ben Eater later turned it into a series of explorable, draggable videos that you should absolutely play with [@eater2018quaternions]. What follows is my own retelling, in my own words and order, of the picture that finally made quaternions click for me.

## A flash of genius on a Dublin bridge

The complex numbers extend the real line into a plane: one real axis, one imaginary axis, and a multiplication that — beautifully — turns out to encode rotation and scaling of that plane. By the 1830s this was understood and loved, and the Irish mathematician William Rowan Hamilton was gripped by the obvious next question: if a two-dimensional number system describes the plane, what is the three-dimensional number system that describes space?

He searched for over a decade. The story goes that his sons would ask at breakfast, "Papa, can you multiply triplets?" and he would shake his head: "No, I can only add and subtract them." The multiplication was the sticking point. You can bolt a second imaginary axis onto the complex numbers easily enough, but every attempt to define a product on those triples broke something essential — division stopped working, or lengths refused to multiply. (It turns out this failure is a theorem, not a lack of cleverness: no three-dimensional number system of the kind Hamilton wanted can exist. That is a story for another post.)

Then, on October 16th, 1843, walking along the Royal Canal in Dublin, Hamilton saw it in a flash: stop looking for one extra imaginary dimension. Add *three*. Three imaginary axes $i$, $j$, $k$ to describe space, bound to one real axis standing perpendicular to all of it, in a fourth dimension. Numbers of the form

$$
q = a + b\,i + c\,j + d\,k, \qquad a, b, c, d \in \mathbb{R},
$$

governed by the relations he famously scratched into the stone of Broom Bridge:

$$
i^2 = j^2 = k^2 = ijk = -1.
$$ {#eq-hamilton}

He called them *quaternions*, and he spent the rest of his life championing them. You have to remember that our modern vector toolkit — dot products, cross products, the word "vector" itself — did not exist yet in standardized form. Hamilton pushed quaternions as *the* language for three-dimensional space, complete with an official society to promote them. The backlash was vicious in a way that is honestly funny to read today: Lord Kelvin wrote that quaternions, "though beautifully ingenious, have been an unmixed evil to those who have touched them in any way." There is even a theory, taken half-seriously by historians, that the Mad Hatter's tea party in *Alice in Wonderland* — written by an Oxford mathematician — is a satire of quaternion multiplication, with the endless rotation around the table mocking its strange, order-sensitive products.

The vector calculus of Gibbs and Heaviside won the textbooks. But the twentieth century staged two rescues. Computer graphics and robotics rediscovered that for representing 3D rotations, quaternions are compact, numerically stable, and free of the pathologies that plague other encodings — your phone, every game engine, and every spacecraft attitude controller multiplies quaternions constantly. And quantum mechanics found that the algebra of quaternions is essentially the algebra of two-state systems: the mathematics of electron spin is Hamilton's discovery wearing a lab coat. By the way, Hamilton coined a word for a quaternion with no real part, a pure combination of $i$, $j$, $k$ describing a point in space. He called it a *vector*. The word you use every day is a fossil of this story.

## Two ways to define the multiplication

Here is the standard way to introduce quaternion multiplication, and there is nothing wrong with it as far as it goes. Take @eq-hamilton, deduce the pairwise products ($ij = k$, $jk = i$, $ki = j$, and the sign flips when you reverse each pair), then multiply any two quaternions by distributing — the same FOIL expansion you would use for complex numbers — and simplifying. This is genuinely how your computer does it, and the fact that the whole operation is a handful of multiply-adds, far cheaper and tidier than the matrix alternative, is a large part of why graphics programmers love it.

But imagine teaching complex numbers this way and *stopping there*: "$i^2 = -1$, distribute, simplify, done." Everything that makes complex numbers feel inevitable — multiplication as rotation, the unit circle as the home of pure turns, $e^{i\theta}$ as a point gliding around it — lives in the geometry, not the symbol-shuffling. The same is true here, except the geometry lives on a sphere in four dimensions. So the real question is: how does anyone *see* such a thing?

## The ladder of empathy

Here is the plan, and it is worth stating in full so you can feel the shape of it. We are three-dimensional creatures trying to see a four-dimensional act. So first, we will try to teach complex number multiplication — a two-dimensional act — to a creature who can only perceive one dimension. Call him Linus the Linelander: his entire universe is a line, his entire algebra is the real numbers. Whatever trick lets Linus "see" the rotation of a plane is a trick we will need, one rung up, for ourselves. Then we will teach the rotation of a sphere — a three-dimensional act — to Felix the Flatlander, who lives in a plane. And then, with both rehearsals behind us, we will stand in their shoes and look at the quaternions. Be generous with your sympathy for Linus and Felix. In a few minutes, you will be them.

### Teaching complex multiplication to a Linelander

First, a way of thinking about complex multiplication that you may already half-know. When you multiply $z \cdot w$, it pays to think of $z$ not as a point but as an *action* — a function that grabs the whole plane and moves it. Which action? Here is the cleanest way to pin it down: every complex number times $0$ is $0$, and every complex number times $1$ is itself. So imagine pinning the plane down at $0$ with one finger, and dragging the point at $1$ over to $z$ with another. There is exactly one stretch-and-rotate motion of the plane that does this, and that motion is "multiplication by $z$." Multiplying by $2$ stretches everything outward by a factor of two. Multiplying by $i$ rotates everything a quarter turn counterclockwise. Multiplying by $-1$ spins the plane half a turn.

Linus can handle the stretching — scaling a line is a perfectly one-dimensional idea. The crisis is rotation. The numbers whose action is a *pure* rotation, no stretch at all, are exactly the ones at distance $1$ from zero: the unit circle. How do you show a circle, and the act of turning it, to someone whose world is a line?

At first glance this seems hopeless — rotation is just intrinsically two-dimensional. But notice: a rotation of the plane has only *one* degree of freedom, the angle. A single number specifies it. So the collection of all pure rotations is, in a meaningful sense, a one-dimensional family, and there ought to be a way to lay it out along Linus's line. The particular way we will use is called **stereographic projection**, and it is the load-bearing construct for everything that follows.

Stand the unit circle in the complex plane and pick the point $-1$ as the projector. For every other point on the circle, draw a straight line from $-1$ through that point, and mark where it crosses the vertical axis through the center. That crossing is the point's shadow on Linus's line. Chase a few landmarks through and the character of the map emerges: the point $1$ projects to the center of the line; $i$ and $-i$ sit *on* the line already, so they stay exactly where they are; the arc between $1$ and $i$ lands in the interval between their shadows. And as you creep around the circle toward $-1$ — from either side — the shadows race off toward the two ends of the line, faster and faster. The point $-1$ itself has no shadow at all: its line never crosses the axis. We say it projects to the *point at infinity*, an idealized point you approach by walking infinitely far along the line in either direction.

Now we hand Linus the projected line, with $1$, $i$, $-i$ marked, and we remind him — this matters — that he is seeing *only the unit circle*, not the whole plane. Numbers like $0$ or $1+i$ or $-2-i$ are simply invisible to him, and that is fine, because today's lesson is only about the pure rotations.

What does Linus see when we multiply everything by $i$? Up in the plane, the circle turns a crisp quarter turn. Down on the line, follow the landmarks: $i \cdot 1 = i$, so the point at the center slides up to where $i$ sits. $i \cdot i = -1$, so the point at $i$ goes shooting off to infinity. $i \cdot (-1) = -i$, so infinity wraps around and comes back in at $-i$ — a point sails off one end of the line and re-enters from beyond the other. And $i \cdot (-i) = 1$, so the point at $-i$ slides up to center. To Linus this is a strange, stretchy, lurching motion. But it is *faithful*: do it four times and every point returns home, which is exactly $i^4 = 1$ made visible. The stretching is an artifact of the projection; the underlying motion is a rigid turn. Keep both of those truths in your head at once — that is the skill this whole post is training.

Take a moment to chew on that before moving on, because we are about to do the same thing one dimension up, and then it will happen *to you*.

### Teaching sphere rotations to a Flatlander

Now for Felix, who lives in a plane and must be shown the rotation of a sphere. To set the stage in a way that will pay off later, let me build the sphere out of number axes. Take the complex plane and add a third axis, perpendicular to both, for a newly invented unit $j$. Points in this three-dimensional space look like $a + b\,i + c\,j$. One arrangement note that will seem fussy now and crucial later: I want the $i$ and $j$ axes lying horizontally — they will play the role of Felix's floor — and the *real* axis standing vertically. The real direction is the one we are always about to sacrifice to the projection, so we orient it out of the plane of the action. (And to repeat the warning from the history: these triples do *not* form a number system; no workable multiplication exists for them. We are using the coordinates only as scaffolding.)

The unit sphere in this space is all points at distance $1$ from zero: $a^2 + b^2 + c^2 = 1$. It passes through six landmarks: $1$ and $-1$ on the real axis, $\pm i$ and $\pm j$ on the floor. Project it stereographically from $-1$, the south pole: for each point of the sphere, draw the line from $-1$ through it, and mark where that line pierces the floor — the $ij$-plane, Felix's world.

The landmarks behave just as they did for Linus, one dimension up. The north pole $1$ lands at the center of Felix's plane. The equator — the circle through $i$, $j$, $-i$, $-j$ — lies in the floor already, so it stays put, every point of it. This is worth underlining: that unit circle is the one honest, undistorted piece of the sphere Felix gets; everything else he sees is shadow. The northern hemisphere (positive real part) projects to the inside of that circle; the southern hemisphere projects outside it, stretching further and further as you approach $-1$, which itself maps to the point at infinity — the point you approach by walking forever in *any* direction across the plane.

Now rotate the sphere and watch through Felix's eyes. The latitude and longitude lines of the sphere project to a lovely shifting family of circles and lines in the plane. And here is a small revelation that buys an enormous amount of intuition: any straight *line* Felix sees is the shadow of a circle on the sphere that passes through $-1$. A line is just a circle that happens to run through infinity. Once you accept that, Felix's whole catalog of shapes — circles and lines — becomes one family, and a rotation that "turns a circle into a line" stops being alarming: up on the sphere, it is just a circle rigidly turning until it passes through the south pole.

Watch one concrete rotation. Spin the sphere $90^\circ$ about the $j$-axis, the turn that carries $1 \to i \to -1 \to -i \to 1$. The circle through those four points — through $1$, $i$, $-1$, $-i$ — projects onto a straight line of Felix's floor, and along that line Felix sees *exactly the lurching motion Linus saw*: center slides out to $i$, $i$ flees to infinity, infinity sneaks back in at $-i$. Felix's view of a sphere rotation literally contains Linus's view of a circle rotation, one slice of it. Meanwhile the honest unit circle on the floor swings up out of the plane — Felix sees his trusted circle deform into a vertical line while a vertical line he had ignored curls into a circle. From outside, you and I can certify that nothing stretched: it is all one rigid turn, reported through a fisheye lens. A rotation about the $i$-axis tells the same story with the roles of $i$ and $j$ swapped, and a rotation about the *real* axis is the one mercy of the projection: Felix just sees his whole plane spin around its center, with only $1$ (at the center) and $-1$ (at infinity) holding still.

If you can hold Felix's picture — honest unit circle, center point $1$, infinity playing the role of $-1$, lines secretly circles — you have done the hard work. Now we climb the last rung.

## The hypersphere of unit quaternions

A quaternion, again, is $q = a + b\,i + c\,j + d\,k$: one real coordinate, three imaginary ones, a point in four-dimensional space. Its size $|q|$ is the square root of the sum of the four squares, exactly as for complex numbers, and sizes multiply: $|q_1 q_2| = |q_1||q_2|$. Multiplying by a general $q$ scales everything by $|q|$ and then performs a very particular kind of four-dimensional rotation. The scaling is Linus-level stuff; the rotation is the prize. And just as the pure rotations of the plane lived on the unit circle, the quaternions whose action is a pure rotation are exactly those of size $1$ — they form the *unit hypersphere*, the set $a^2+b^2+c^2+d^2=1$, a three-dimensional surface curving through four-dimensional space.

You cannot see that. Neither can I. But we have rehearsed precisely this predicament twice, so we do to ourselves what we did to Felix: stereographic projection, from $-1$, one dimension up. Every unit quaternion other than $-1$ gets a definite position in our ordinary 3D space, and the landmarks land exactly where the ladder predicts:

The number $1$ projects to the very center of our space. The sphere through $i$, $j$, $k$ and their negatives — the "equator" of the hypersphere, all the unit quaternions with zero real part, Hamilton's pure vectors — lies in our space already and projects to *itself*: an honest, undistorted unit sphere sitting around the origin. Everything else we see is shadow: unit quaternions with positive real part project to the inside of that sphere, crowding toward $1$ at the center; those with negative real part project outside it; and $-1$ is our point at infinity, reachable by walking forever in any direction. One more dictionary entry carries up from Felix's world: any flat *plane* we see through the origin is secretly a great sphere of the hypersphere passing through $-1$, and any straight *line* through landmarks is secretly a circle through $-1$. The line through $1$ (center), $i$, and $-i$ that we see in our space *is* the unit circle of the complex plane, projected; the whole complex plane's unit of rotation is one thin thread of this picture.

Pause here. Everything visible in this 3D picture — the honest sphere, the crowded interior, the sparse exterior — is a single curved 3D surface in 4D, seen through a fisheye. Every point of it is at distance exactly $1$ from a number zero that is *nowhere in the picture at all*. When you are comfortable with that sentence, read on.

## Multiplication: two rotations, locked together

Now the payoff. What does left-multiplication by a unit quaternion do to this hypersphere? Here is the answer in one sentence, the sentence this whole post exists to make meaningful:

> Multiplying on the left by a unit quaternion $q$ rotates the circle through $1$, $q$, $-1$ so as to carry $1$ to $q$ — and simultaneously rotates the circle *perpendicular* to it by the same angle, with the direction given by a right-hand rule.

Two perpendicular circles, turning in lockstep. That is a motion which simply has no room to exist in three dimensions — in 3D, a rotation has an axis, a line of fixed points, and this motion fixes nothing at all. In four dimensions it is the most natural thing in the world. Let's make it concrete.

**Multiplication by $i$.** The circle through $1$ and $i$ (and $-1$, at infinity) appears to us as a straight line through the origin. Along it we see Linus's lurch yet again: $1 \to i$, $i \to -1$ (off to infinity), $-1 \to -i$ (back in from beyond), $-i \to 1$. A $90^\circ$ rotation, faithfully fisheyed. But now look at the circle through $j$ and $k$, lying on the honest unit sphere. In four dimensions it is exactly perpendicular to the $1i$-circle — two circles with the same center, the same radius, and not a single point of contact, a configuration that sounds absurd until you remember they have four dimensions to dodge each other in. The rule: point your right thumb along the visible line from $1$ toward $i$, and curl your fingers. The $jk$-circle turns the way your fingers curl, through the same $90^\circ$. So $j \to k$, $k \to -j$, $-j \to -k$, $-k \to j$. Read off the products:

$$
i \cdot 1 = i, \quad i \cdot i = -1, \quad i \cdot j = k, \quad i \cdot k = -j.
$$

My honest hope is that this is not a table you memorize but a motion you can close your eyes and *watch*: the line through the origin flowing, the perpendicular circle rolling with your curled fingers. And because multiplication distributes, knowing what happens to $1, i, j, k$ — a basis for the whole 4D space — pins down what happens to every quaternion. In the language of linear algebra: know the transformation on a basis and you know it everywhere. Do this motion four times and everything comes home: $i^4 = 1$, now in stereo.

**A general unit quaternion.** Take $q = -\tfrac{\sqrt2}{2} + \tfrac{\sqrt2}{2}\,i$, which lives on the $1i$-circle at $135^\circ$ from $1$ — negative real part, so its projection sits *outside* the honest sphere, out along the $i$ direction. (If that placement feels odd, ask how Linus would have drawn it.) Left-multiplication by $q$ drags $1$ along the visible line out to $q$'s position, while the perpendicular $jk$-circle rolls $135^\circ$ by the right-hand rule. The recipe is fully general: for any unit quaternion $q$, draw the circle through $1$, $q$, $-1$ (you see it as a line or circle through the origin); rotate it to carry $1 \to q$; find the perpendicular circle on the honest sphere; turn it the same amount, right-handedly. One number's worth of choice — which is to say, a point on the hypersphere — and the motion is locked.

## Order matters, and that is a feature

Compute $i \cdot j$ with the picture: thumb from $1$ to $i$, curl, and $j$ rolls to $k$. Now compute $j \cdot i$: thumb from $1$ to $j$, curl, and $i$ rolls to $-k$. So

$$
ij = k, \qquad ji = -k.
$$

Quaternion multiplication is not commutative, and rather than an embarrassment, this is the signature of what quaternions *are*. Composition of rotations in space genuinely does not commute: turn a book a quarter turn about the vertical axis and then a quarter turn about an axis through its spine, and you get a different result than in the other order — try it with the nearest book, it never stops being surprising. Solving a Rubik's cube, order matters. Commutativity is a far more special property than our childhood arithmetic led us to believe, and a number system honest enough to describe spatial rotation *had* to give it up. The Mad Hatter can laugh all he likes.

One refinement, and it is the doorway to the sequel. Everything above treated $q$ as acting from the *left*: in $i \cdot j$, the $i$ does the moving and the $j$ gets moved. You can equally well read it as $j$ acting on $i$ from the *right* — and right-multiplication is the same kind of double rotation with one elegant change: the perpendicular circle obeys a *left*-hand rule instead. Either hand computes $ij = k$; they disagree about other things, and that disagreement is not a bug but a resource.

Why care? Because a single quaternion multiplication, for all its beauty, does *not* directly give a rotation of 3D space — look at the picture: multiplying by $i$ does not carry the honest $ijk$-sphere to itself, it tips that sphere off through the fourth dimension. The actual recipe for rotating a 3D vector $v$ is the famous sandwich $q\,v\,q^{-1}$ — a left action and a right action conspiring, one hand against the other, so that the off-sphere tilts cancel and what survives is a clean rotation of the honest sphere. Unpacking that sandwich, and the lovely surprise hiding in it (each rotation has *two* quaternion names, $q$ and $-q$ — the "double cover" that quantum mechanics cares about), deserves a post of its own, and it will get one.

For now, sit with the picture you have earned: a hypersphere none of us can see, projected into the space we can; an honest unit sphere of Hamilton's vectors; the number $1$ at the heart of everything and $-1$ everywhere at infinity; and multiplication as two perpendicular circles turning together, your right thumb pointing the way. Then go play with Sanderson and Eater's explorable versions [@eater2018quaternions], where you can drag the hypersphere around yourself — these pictures are best believed through the fingertips. Doesn't it feel good when an "unmixed evil" turns out to be geometry, patiently waiting a century and a half for someone to draw it?
